headline: デモ is a clipped デモンストレーション, and Korean has a form 데모 to compare.
“Preceding” is “go before” — and the same spelling has a native reading, sakiyuki, from 1678.
“Splendid” is “seeing” plus “thing”, first cited in 1309.
“A way of doing” is built from the stem of する and “method”.
A vase is a “flower jar” in Chinese — and a native reading of the same spelling used an “earthenware pot”.
The “stomach” was a deliberately indirect word for “belly”, spelled with a character that means something else.
Gravity borrowed an old Chinese word for “heavy strength” and repurposed it to translate a Dutch one.
“Ugly” is, word for word, “hard to look at”.
A lighter and a writer are the same word in katakana.
“Usually” was written 不断 first — the kanji we use now were fitted to the sound.
“New” began as “freshly coming into being”.
“Do your best” once meant “be stubborn” — and the 頑 may belong to neither candidate origin.
A fountain pen is a “ten-thousand-year pen”.
A pocket notebook is a “hand ledger”, in use from the early 1600s.
“Enormous” is “swell” plus “big”, and the word is first attested in 1872.
To be dented is to have “lessened inward” — herikomu worn down to hekomu.
A truck has a twin in トロッコ, and a running track shares its spelling.
A fault is a “lacking point”, borrowed from Chinese.
“Perhaps” is a clipped phrase whose first half is still being argued over.
An honorific “eat” is “take” plus “rise up” — each already honorific.
The newspaper is a Chinese “new hearing” — and in Japanese it began as a clipping of “newspaper paper”.
“Word” is an old “word” plus an “edge” — and the 葉 in the spelling is only a stand-in.
Geta are “lower clogs” — and the “footwear” sense of 駄 may exist only in Japan.
A snowstorm is a verb's stem — and the spelling was borrowed from Chinese for its meaning.
The train platform and the home are two different clippings of two English words.
“The future” began as a Buddhist calque of a Sanskrit phrase for “not yet come”.
A smile is a “laughing face”, with かお voiced to がお.
To recall is to “take out” a thought.
Electricity was borrowed from Chinese in the 1850s; “electric light” is a 1901 contraction.
“Mother” in two layers: a surface of “honorific, mother, honorific”, and under it the older o-kaka-sama.
A hot spring is “warm spring” in Chinese — and the old /wonsen/ lost its w.
